slides.title: Unit Outline
slides.body:
Unit Outline

Part 1: Anatomical and functional organization of the nervous system
Part 2: Nervous tissue
Part 3: The central nervous system

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
In this unit, we will begin by discussing the organization of the nervous system as a whole. We will then zoom in to examine nervous tissue, before zooming back out to examine the central nervous system. 

Subsequent units will examine the neuronal signalling and the peripheral nervous system.

slides.title: Part 1: Anatomical and functional organization of the nervous system
slides.body:
Part 1: Anatomical and functional organization of the nervous system

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: We begin with Part 1: Anatomical and functional organization of the nervous system.

slides.title: Part 1: Anatomical and functional organization of the nervous system
slides.body:
Part 1: Anatomical and functional organization of the nervous system

Anatomical Divisions
central nervous system (CNS)
brain and spinal cord
peripheral nervous system (PNS)
nerves and ganglia

Central and Peripheral Nervous System. The structures of the peripheral nervous system are referred to as ganglia and nerves, which can be seen as distinct structures. The equivalent structures in the central nervous system are not obvious from this overall perspective and are best examined in prepared tissue under the microscope.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
The nervous system is a complex structure, responsible for many different functions.

If we start with a basic overview, we can divide the nervous system into two major regions: the central and the peripheral nervous systems. The central nervous system (CNS) is the brain and spinal cord, and the peripheral nervous system (PNS) is everything else.

The brain is contained within the cranial cavity of the skull, and the spinal cord is contained within the vertebral cavity of the vertebral column. Most, though not all of the PNS elements are outside of these two cavities.

Various types of neurons. Credit: Miguel Iglesias, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Nervous tissue of both the central and peripheral nervous systems contains two basic types of cells: neurons and glia. 

Glial cells (also called glia or neuroglia) are one of a variety of cells that provide a framework of tissue that supports the neurons and their activities. 

The neuron is the more functionally important of the two, in terms of the communicative function of the nervous system. However, neurons do range quite a bit in their own structure and function.

Parts of a Neuron. The major parts of the neuron are labeled on a multipolar neuron from the central nervous system.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
To describe the functional divisions of the nervous system, it is important to understand the structure of a neuron. Neurons are cells and therefore have a soma, or cell body, but they also have extensions of the cell; each extension is generally referred to as a process. 

There is one important process that every neuron has called an axon, which is the fiber that connects a neuron with its target. 

Another type of process that branches off from the soma is the dendrite. Dendrites are responsible for receiving most of the input from other neurons.

slides.title: Part 1: Anatomical and functional organization of the nervous system
slides.body:
Part 1: Anatomical and functional organization of the nervous system

Grey matter
primarily soma (and dendrites)
pinkish if blood present
White matter
primarily axons
white due to myelin on axons

Grey Matter and White Matter. A brain removed during an autopsy, with a partial section removed, shows white matter surrounded by grey matter. grey matter makes up the outer cortex of the brain. (credit: modification of work by “Suseno”/ Wikimedia Commons)

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Looking at nervous tissue, there are regions that predominantly contain cell bodies and regions that are largely composed of just axons.

These two regions within nervous system structures are often referred to as grey matter (the regions with many cell bodies and dendrites) or white matter (the regions with many axons). The colors ascribed to these regions are what would be seen in “fresh,” or unstained, nervous tissue. Grey matter is not necessarily grey. It can be pinkish because of blood content, or even slightly tan, depending on how long the tissue has been preserved. But white matter is white because axons are insulated by a lipid-rich substance called myelin. Lipids can appear as white (“fatty”) material, much like the fat on a raw piece of chicken or beef.

slides.title: Part 1: Anatomical and functional organization of the nervous system
slides.body:
Part 1: Anatomical and functional organization of the nervous system

Nucleus
cluster of cell bodies within CNS
Ganglion
cluster of cell bodies in PNS

What Is a Nucleus? (a) The nucleus of an atom contains its protons and neutrons. (b) The nucleus of a cell is the organelle that contains DNA. (c) A nucleus in the central nervous system is a localized center of function with the cell bodies of several neurons, shown here circled in red. (credit c: “Was a bee”/Wikimedia Commons)

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Discrete anatomical structures also need to be named. Those names are specific to whether the structure is central or peripheral. 

A localized collection of neuron cell bodies in the central nervous system is referred to as a nucleus. In the peripheral nervous system, a cluster of neuron cell bodies is referred to as a ganglion 

The term nucleus has a few different meanings within anatomy and physiology. It is the center of an atom, where protons and neutrons are found; it is the center of a cell, where the DNA is found; and it is a center of some function in the central nervous system. 

There is also a potentially confusing use of the word ganglion (plural = ganglia) that has a historical explanation. In the central nervous system, there is a group of nuclei that are connected together and were once called the basal ganglia before “ganglion” became accepted as a description for a peripheral structure. Some sources refer to this group of nuclei as the “basal nuclei” to avoid confusion.

slides.body:
Part 1: Anatomical and functional organization of the nervous system

Tract
bundle of axons in CNS
e.g., optic tract
Nerve
bundle of axons in PNS
e.g., optic nerve
note that these are the same bundles of axons as optic tract!

Optic Nerve Versus Optic Tract. This drawing of the connections of the eye to the brain shows the optic nerve extending from the eye to the chiasm, where the structure continues as the optic tract. The same axons extend from the eye to the brain through these two bundles of fibers, but the chiasm represents the border between peripheral and central.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Terminology applied to bundles of axons also differs depending on location. A bundle of axons, or fibers, found in the central nervous system is called a tract whereas the same thing in the peripheral nervous system would be called a nerve. 

There is an important point to make about these terms, which is that they can both be used to refer to the same bundle of axons. The most obvious example of this is the axons that project from the retina into the brain. Those axons are called the optic nerve as they leave the eye, but when they are inside the cranium, they are referred to as the optic tract. There is a specific place where the name changes, which is the optic chiasm, but they are still the same axons. This is much like how some roads change names as they transition from one city to another.

slides.title: Part 1: Anatomical and functional organization of the nervous system

Part 1: Anatomical and functional organization of the nervous system

Functional divisions
sensation
integration
response
somatic
autonomic

The Functional Organization of the Nervous System. The diagram represents the divisions of the nervous system involved in each of the basic functions: sensation (receiving and processing information from the external and internal environment), integration (comparing the sensory input with stored information and with other sensory inputs in order for the body to react appropriately) and response (most commonly, a motor command generated by the somatic nervous system or the autonomic nervous system).

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Functional Divisions

There are two ways to consider how the nervous system is divided functionally. First, the basic functions of the nervous system are sensation, integration, and response. Secondly, control of the body can be somatic or autonomic—divisions that are largely defined by the structures that are involved in the response. There is also a region of the peripheral nervous system that is called the enteric nervous system that is responsible for a specific set of the functions within the realm of autonomic control related to gastrointestinal functions. However, the enteric nervous system is often clumped in together with the autonomic nervous system.

slides.title: Part 1: Anatomical and functional organization of the nervous system
slides.body:
Part 1: Anatomical and functional organization of the nervous system

Sensation
registers external (or internal) stimulus
Integration
stimuli compared with other stimuli, memories, and state of person at a particular time
Response
somatic nervous system (SNS)
voluntary motor responses of skeletal muscle
reflexes (without conscious decision to perform them)
autonomic nervous system (ANS)
involuntary control of the body, usually for the sake of homeostasis
motor output extends to smooth and cardiac muscle as well as glandular tissue
physiological responses tied to emotional states
enteric nervous system (ENS)
controlling the smooth muscle and glandular tissue in your digestive system
sometimes considered part of the autonomic system

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
The nervous system is involved in receiving information about the environment around us (sensation) and generating responses to that information. But there is a third function that needs to be included. Sensory input needs to be integrated with other sensations, as well as with memories, emotional state, or learning. Some regions of the nervous system are termed integration or association areas. The process of integration combines sensory perceptions and higher cognitive functions such as memories, learning, and emotion to produce a response.

The first major function of the nervous system is sensation—receiving information about the environment to gain input about what is happening outside the body (or, sometimes, within the body). The sensory functions of the nervous system register the presence of a particular event in the external or internal environment, known as a stimulus. The senses we think of most are the “big five”: taste, smell, touch, sight, and hearing. The stimuli for taste and smell are both chemical substances (molecules, compounds, ions, etc.), touch is physical or mechanical stimuli that interact with the skin, sight is light stimuli, and hearing is the perception of sound, which is a physical stimulus similar to some aspects of touch. There are actually more senses than just those, but that list represents the major senses. Those five are all senses that receive stimuli from the outside world, and of which there is conscious perception. Additional sensory stimuli might be from the internal environment (inside the body), such as the stretch of an organ wall or the concentration of certain ions in the blood.

Stimuli that are received by sensory structures are communicated to the nervous system where that information is processed. This is called integration. Stimuli are compared with, or integrated with, other stimuli, memories of previous stimuli, or the state of a person at a particular time. This leads to the specific response that will be generated. For example, in baseball, when deciding whether to swing or not, the batter needs to consider the trajectory of the ball, its speed, the pitch count, whether anyone is on base, etc.

The nervous system produces a response on the basis of the stimuli perceived by sensory structures. An obvious response would be the movement of muscles, such as withdrawing a hand from a hot stove, but there are broader uses of the term. The nervous system can cause the contraction of all three types of muscle tissue. For example, skeletal muscle contracts to move the skeleton, cardiac muscle is influenced as heart rate increases during exercise, and smooth muscle contracts as the digestive system moves food along the digestive tract. Responses also include the neural control of glands in the body as well, such as the production and secretion of sweat by the eccrine and apocrine sweat glands found in the skin to lower body temperature.

Responses can be divided into those that are voluntary or conscious (like contraction of skeletal muscle) and those that are involuntary (like contraction of smooth muscles, regulation of cardiac muscle, activation of glands, etc.). 

The nervous system can thus be divided into two parts mostly on the basis of a functional difference in responses. The somatic nervous system is responsible for voluntary motor responses involving skeletal muscle. But those contractions are not always voluntary in the sense that you have to want to perform them. Some somatic motor responses are reflexes, and often happen without a conscious decision to perform them. 

The autonomic nervous system is responsible for involuntary control of the body, usually for the sake of homeostasis. Sensory input for autonomic functions can be from sensory structures tuned to external or internal environmental stimuli. The motor output extends to smooth and cardiac muscle as well as glandular tissue. The role of the autonomic system is to regulate the organ systems of the body, which usually means to control homeostasis. Sweat glands, for example, are controlled by the autonomic system. When you are hot, sweating helps cool your body down. That is a homeostatic mechanism. But when you are nervous, you might start sweating also. That is not homeostatic, it is the physiological response to an emotional state.

There is another division of the nervous system that describes functional responses. The enteric nervous system is responsible for controlling the smooth muscle and glandular tissue in your digestive system. It is a large part of the peripheral nervous system, and is not dependent on the central nervous system. It is sometimes valid, however, to consider the enteric system to be a part of the autonomic system because the neural structures that make up the enteric system are a component of the autonomic output that regulates digestion. There are some differences between the two, but for our purposes here there will be a good bit of overlap.

Glia (Greek for “glue”)

Parts of a Neuron. The major parts of the neuron are labeled on a multipolar neuron from the central nervous system.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
As mentioned earlier, nervous tissue is composed of two types of cells: neurons and glia. Let’s now look at these in a bit more detail.

Neurons  are responsible for the computation and communication that the nervous system provides. They are electrically active and release chemical signals to target cells. 

Neurons are the primary type of cell that most anyone associates with the nervous system – they get most of the attention. Although at first glance, this image seems to be that of a neuron – and even its caption suggests this notion – the image actually also contains a glial cell. This oligodendrocyte – a type of glial cell – forms the myelin sheath around the axon of the neuron. Glia do not get as much attention as neurons, but they are equally as important.

Glial cells, also called neuroglial or just glia, comprise almost 50% of the cells in the human brain. The name glia comes from the Greek word that means “glue”. As this name implies, glia are known to play a supporting role for nervous tissue – holding things together. However, we now know that glia serve many important functions, and recent research even suggests that glia themselves might play a direct role in signaling, although neurons are still considered the basis of this function.

slides.body:
Part 2: Nervous tissue

Neurons
soma
contains nucleus and most major organelles
processes
one axon
starts at axon hillock
propagates action potential (from hillock)
can branch
axon terminals project to target cells
(usually) wrapped in myelin
speeds APs 
possesses nodes of Ranvier (regenerates APs)
dendrites

usually highly branched
information flow: dendrites → soma → axon

Parts of a Neuron. The major parts of the neuron are labeled on a multipolar neuron from the central nervous system.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
As you learned in the first section, the main part of a neuron is the cell body, which is usually referred to the soma (soma means “body”). 

The soma contains the nucleus and most of the major organelles. But what makes neurons special is that they have many extensions of their cell membranes, which are generally referred to as processes. 

Neurons are usually described as having one, and only one, axon—a fibre that emerges from the cell body and projects to target cells. That single axon can branch repeatedly to communicate with many target cells. It is the axon that propagates the nerve impulse, which is communicated to one or more cells. Where the axon emerges from the cell body, there is a special region referred to as the axon hillock. This is a tapering of the cell body toward the axon fibre. Within the axon hillock, the cytoplasm changes to a solution of limited components called axoplasm. 

The other processes of the neuron are dendrites, which receive information from other neurons at specialized areas of contact called synapses. The dendrites are usually highly branched processes, providing locations for other neurons to communicate with the cell body. Information flows through a neuron from the dendrites, across the cell body, and down the axon. This gives the neuron a polarity—meaning that information flows in this one direction.

Many axons are wrapped by an insulating substance called myelin, which is actually made from glial cells. Myelin acts as insulation much like the plastic or rubber that is used to insulate electrical wires. A key difference between myelin and the insulation on a wire is that there are gaps in the myelin covering of an axon. Each gap is called a node of Ranvier and is important to the way that electrical signals travel down the axon – it is where action potentials are regenerated so they don’t fade out. The length of the axon between each gap, which is wrapped in myelin, is referred to as an axon segment. At the end of the axon is the axon terminal, where there are usually several branches extending toward the target cell, each of which ends at a synapse.

slides.title: Part 2: Nervous tissue
slides.body:
Part 2: Nervous tissue

Types of neurons
billions of neurons in NS
many types of neurons
classification based on number of processes:
unipolar
bipolar
multipolar
classifications also based on:
shape
location
function
who discovered them

Neuron Classification by Shape. Unipolar cells have one process that includes both the axon and dendrite. Bipolar cells have two processes, the axon and a dendrite. Multipolar cells have more than two processes, the axon and two or more dendrites.

Other Neuron Classifications. Three examples of neurons that are classified on the basis of other criteria. (a) The pyramidal cell is a multipolar cell with a cell body that is shaped something like a pyramid. (b) The Purkinje cell in the cerebellum was named after the scientist who originally described it. (c) Olfactory neurons are named for the functional group with which they belong.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Types of Neurons

There are billions of neurons in the nervous system. And there are many different types of neurons. They can be classified by many different criteria. The first way to classify them is by the number of processes attached to the cell body. Using the standard model of neurons, one of these processes is the axon, and the rest are dendrites. Hence, in the top figure here, you can see a unipolar neuron, with only one process, an axon, extending from the cell body but then splitting, so that one end serves as a cluster of dendrites while the other end acts as an axon terminus. A bipolar neuron also has dendrites and an axon, but the dendrites do not connect immediately to the cell some, but rather to a projection of the soma. A multipolar neuron has many short processes leaving the cell soma, each ending in dendrites, plus one axon.

Neurons can also be classified on the basis of their shape, where they are found, who found them, what they do, or even what chemicals they use to communicate with each other. Some neurons in the bottom figure are named on the basis of such classifications. For example, a multipolar neuron that has a very important role to play in a part of the brain called the cerebellum is known as a Purkinje cell. It is named after the anatomist who discovered it, Jan Purkinje, who I enjoy highlighting, as he was born on the outskirts of Prague, in the Czech Republic, where I was born.

Glial Cells of the Central Nervous System. The central nervous system has astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, microglia, and ependymal cells that support the neurons of the central nervous system in several ways.

Part 2: Nervous tissue

Glia
CNS
astrocytes
envelop and regulate synapses; provide nutrients to neurons; help form blood-brain barrier
microglia
immune cells, phagocytes
ependymal cells
line ventricles; filter blood to create cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)
oligodendrocytes (a.k.a., oligodendroglia)
produce myelin
PNS
satellite cells
envelop and nourish neurons in ganglia
Schwann cells
produce myelin

Glial Cells of the Peripheral Nervous System. The peripheral nervous system has satellite cells and Schwann cells.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Glial Cells

There are six types of glial cells in the nervous system. Four of them are found in the central nervous system and two are found in the peripheral nervous system. 

Astrocytes, named for their star shape, help surround synapses and regulate their contents of ions, released neurotransmitters, etc. They also help provide nutrients to neurons. And they envelop blood vessels in the brain to help form the blood-brain-barrier, which protects the brain from blood contaminants that may have entered the rest of the body.

Microglia are cells of the immune system, found in the central nervous system. They patrol the central nervous system, and phagocytose pathogens and damaged cells.

Ependymal cells filter blood to create the cerebrospinal fluid, or CSF, that is found within the central nervous system.

Myelin, the insulation for axons, is provided by oligodendrocytes (also called oligodendroglia) in the central nervous system, and Schwann cells in the peripheral nervous system. As mentioned already, myelin is a lipid-rich sheath that surrounds the axon and by doing so facilitates the transmission of electrical signals along the axon. The lipids are essentially the phospholipids of the glial cell membrane. 

Finally, satellite cells surround ganglia in the peripheral nervous system, providing nutrients and support to those neurons.

The spinal cord is a single structure, whereas the adult brain is described in terms of four major regions: the cerebrum, the diencephalon, the brain stem, and the cerebellum.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: Developmentally, the brain forms three primary vesicles: the forebrain, the midbrain, and the hindbrain. Most vertebrate brains look like the developmental diagrams in the top figure. In mammals, and especially humans, the cerebrum grows much more than the other regions and forms the largest part of the brain. Note that the cerebrum and diencephalon are both part of the forebrain. The midbrain and two parts of the hindbrain, the pons and the medulla oblongata form the brainstem, because they look like a stem holding up the forebrain. The cerebellum is also part of the hindbrain, but it sits behind the brain stem.

slides.title: Part 3: The central nervous system
slides.body:
Part 3: The central nervous system

Cerebrum

R and L hemispheres
superficial layer of cell somas on outside, with axons deep

The Cerebrum. The cerebrum is a large component of the central nervous system in humans, and the most obvious aspect of it is the folded surface called the cerebral cortex. Deep within the cerebrum, the white matter of the corpus callosum provides the major pathway for communication between the two hemispheres of the cerebral cortex.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
The Cerebrum

The large, anterior part of the human brain is the cerebrum, with two distinct halves, a right and a left cerebral hemisphere. Many of the higher neurological functions, such as memory, emotion, and consciousness, are the result of cerebral function. The cerebrum comprises the cerebral cortex, a continuous, wrinkled and thin layer of grey matter that wraps around both hemispheres, and several subcortical nuclei. A gyrus (plural = gyri) is the ridge of one of those wrinkles, and a sulcus (plural = sulci) is the groove between two gyri. 

The head is limited by the size of the birth canal, and the brain must fit inside the cranial cavity of the skull. Extensive folding in the cerebral cortex enables more gray matter to fit into this limited space. If the gray matter of the cortex were peeled off of the cerebrum and laid out flat, its surface area would be roughly equal to one square meter.

Different regions of the cerebral cortex can be associated with particular functions, a concept known as localization of function. 

The occipital lobe is responsible for primary visual perception. That visual information is complex, so it is processed in the temporal and parietal lobes as well.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: The temporal lobe is associated with primary auditory sensation, including the understanding of language. There is also some visual processing present – the ventral stream of the visual pathway from the occipital cortex, processing information such as object recognition. Because subcortical regions of the temporal lobe are part of the limbic system, including the hippocampus and amygdala, memory is also an important function associated with that lobe. Memory is essentially a sensory function; memories are recalled sensations such as the smell of baking or the sound of a barking dog. Even memories of movement are really the memory of sensory feedback from those movements, such as stretching muscles or the movement of the skin around a joint. Structures in the temporal lobe are responsible for establishing long-term memory, but the ultimate location of those memories is usually in the region in which the sensory perception was processed.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: The main sensation associated with the parietal lobe is somatosensation, meaning the general sensations associated with the body. Posterior to the central sulcus is the postcentral gyrus, the primary somatosensory cortex. All of the tactile senses are processed in this area, including touch, pressure, tickle, pain, itch, and vibration, as well as more general senses of the body such as proprioception and kinesthesia, which are the senses of body position and movement, respectively. The most caudal portions of the parietal lobe, those in contact with the occipital lobe, possess the dorsal stream of the visual system, and help to process visual information, especially that pertaining to the movement of objects, or their position in space.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Anterior to the central sulcus is the frontal lobe, which is associated with motor functions and higher cognitive activities like decision-making. The precentral gyrus is the primary motor cortex. Cells from this region of the cerebral cortex are the upper motor neurons that instruct cells in the spinal cord to move skeletal muscles. 

Anterior to this region are a few areas that are associated with planned movements. The premotor area is responsible for thinking of a movement to be made. 

Broca’s area is responsible for the production of language, or controlling movements responsible for speech; in the vast majority of people, it is located only on the left side. 

Anterior to these regions is the prefrontal lobe, which serves cognitive functions that can be the basis of personality, short-term memory, and consciousness. The prefrontal lobotomy is an outdated mode of treatment for personality disorders.

Prefrontal cortex damage in Phineas Gage case study. Adapted from: Database Center for Life Science(DBCLS)[2], CC BY-SA 2.1 JP, via Wikimedia Commons

Phineas Gage. Credit: Originally from the collection of Jack and Beverly Wilgus, and now in the Warren Anatomical Museum, Harvard Medical School., CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: Probably the most famous case study of anterior frontal cortex function (not the motor parts, but the cognitive parts) involves that of Phineas Gage. Phineas was an American railroad construction foreman who survived an accident when tamping down blasting powder into a deep hole, using an iron tamping rod. A spark ignited the blasting powder and propelled the rod through Phineas’ skull, damaging the anterior part of his left frontal cortex. After recovering from the accident, and for years, until other parts of his brain seemed to take over the lost functions of his damaged prefrontal cortex, Phineas was described as having a changed personality, whereby he was much more argumentative, profane, and unreliable than before the accident. Some of his behavioral changes seem to have been exaggerated over time, but it does seem that his personality was substantially changed by damage to this brain region; and whether the changes were as large as some claim, or not, this case study is not easily forgotten, and thus serves as a valuable learning tool for brain function.

Frontal Section of Cerebral Cortex and Basal Nuclei. The major components of the basal nuclei, shown in a frontal section of the brain, are the caudate (just lateral to the lateral ventricle), the putamen (inferior to the caudate and separated by the large white-matter structure called the internal capsule), and the globus pallidus (medial to the putamen).

Hippocampus and Amygdala. Adapted from: Miserlou, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Beneath the cerebral cortex are sets of nuclei known as subcortical nuclei that augment cortical processes. The hippocampus and amygdala are medial-lobe structures that, along with the adjacent cortex, are involved in long-term memory formation and emotional responses. The basal nuclei are a set of nuclei in the cerebrum responsible for comparing cortical processing with the general state of activity in the nervous system to influence the likelihood of movement taking place. The basal nuclei used to be referred to as the basal ganglia, and you may still see this term used, but is can lead to confusion because the term ganglia is typically used for peripheral structures.

The major structures of the basal nuclei that control movement are the caudate, putamen, and globus pallidus, which are located deep in the cerebrum. Together, the caudate and putamen are called the striatum. The globus pallidus lies just medial to the putamen. These nuclei are depicted in a frontal section of the brain in the figure here, but you do not have to memorize their individual names – just that they are part of the basal nuclei.

Cerebrum
hippocampal damage
Henry Gustav Molaison (H.M.)
surgery in 1953

Hippocampus. Credit: Miserlou, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: One of the most fascinating case studies pertaining to that of the role of the hippocampus in memory formation, is that of Henry Gustav Molaison, more famously known as patient H.M. – during his lifetime he was only known by his initials in order to protect his identity. HM suffered from debilitating epilepsy that did not respond to drug treatments. Hence, as a last resort, surgeons removed tissue, bilaterally – from both hemispheres – at the site where the seizures started. This happened to be the hippocampus and the surrounding regions. Although the procedure did help control his epilepsy, it resulted in HM losing the ability to form new memories. He remembered his past life quite well – those memories had already been consolidated into long-term memories, which we already mentioned are housed throughout the cerebral cortices, in locations corresponding to the processing of their sensory modality (vision, sound, smell, etc.). However, the hippocampus is necessary for the formation of short-term memories; without it, he would forget a person as soon as he met them. Nurses and doctors that worked with him for decades would need to reintroduce themselves every minute or two, for the rest of his life. And because he could form no new short-term memories, they could not be converted to long-term memories. He was stuck in 1953 for the rest of his life, until his death in 2008.

slides.body:
Part 3: The central nervous system

Corpus callosum
white matter bridge (commissure) between cerebral hemispheres
split brain patients reveal how the two hemispheres act as independent brains, but normally communicate with one another

Corpus callosum. Adapted from: Life Science Databases(LSDB)., CC BY-SA 2.1 JP, via Wikimedia Commons

Corpus callosum. Credit: modified image created by user:Looie496.  original images created by John A. Beal, Ph.D., CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons
slides.notes:
The two cerebral hemispheres are connected by “bridges” of white matter, called commissures. The most prominent of these is the corpus callosum. These commissures allow the left and right sides of the cerebral cortex to communicate with one another.

A fascinating example of how your two cerebral hemispheres are actually two entities, working together, is that of split-brain patients. Much like the case of HM, these patients had severe epilepsy that could only be treated with the removal of brain tissue. Unlike HM, where grey matter in the hippocampal region was removed, split brain patients have the corpus callosum cut, at least partly, breaking the axonal connections between hemispheres; these connections were allowing the overstimulation that causes seizures to spread back and forth between the hemispheres, causing out-of-control overstimulation.

Because the right side of the brain controls the left side of the body, and vice versa, there are documented cases where split-brain patients perform opposing actions with each hand, such as one trying to pull up pants, while the other hand pulls them down. When such patients are shown images in only heir left visual field, they cannot name those images, as they are only “seen” by the right hemisphere, and it is the left hemisphere, and Broca’s area, which is usually responsible for language production. Even more fascinating, you can present a word prompt in the left visual field, to the right hemisphere, telling the patient to go take a washroom break; but if you then ask the patient why they are getting up, the (verbal) left hemisphere confabulates an answer, with the patient stating something like: “Oh I just wanted to get up and stretch my legs”. These confabulations are not just a solitary incident – they have been reported across many split-brain patients. The brain is a fascinating organ! 

I’ve included a link to a video on split brain patients in the course materials, if you want to learn more about this topic.

Olfactory bulbs and nerves. Adapted from: Database Center for Life Science(DBCLS)[2], CC BY-SA 2.1 JP, via Wikimedia Commons

Diencephalon stem. Adapted from: Images are generated by Life Science Databases(LSDB), CC BY-SA 2.1 JP, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Okay, let’s now move from the cerebrum down to the diencephalon.

The word diencephalon translates to “through brain.” It is the connection between the cerebrum and the rest of the nervous system, with one exception. The rest of the brain, the spinal cord, and the peripheral nervous system all send information to the cerebrum through the diencephalon. Output from the cerebrum passes through the diencephalon. The single exception is the system associated with olfaction, or the sense of smell, which connects directly with the cerebrum.

slides.title: Part 3: The central nervous system
slides.body:
Part 3: The central nervous system

Diencephalon
thalamus
collection of brain nuclei; process and relay sensory information to cerebrum
conscious perception
sends motor commands down from cerebrum
hypothalamus
collection of brain nuclei; inferior to thalamus
regulates homeostasis - eating, thirst, body temperature
regulates autonomic nervous system
regulates (much of) endocrine system through anterior pituitary gland

regulates circadian rhythms (day/night)

The Diencephalon. The diencephalon is composed primarily of the thalamus and hypothalamus, which together define the walls of the third ventricle. The thalami are two elongated, ovoid structures on either side of the midline that make contact in the middle. The hypothalamus is inferior and anterior to the thalamus, culminating in a sharp angle to which the pituitary gland is attached.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
The two major regions of the diencephalon are the thalamus and the hypothalamus. 

The thalamus is a collection of nuclei that relay information between the cerebral cortex and the periphery, spinal cord, or brain stem. All sensory information, except for the sense of smell, passes through the thalamus before processing by the cortex. Axons from the peripheral sensory organs, or intermediate nuclei, synapse in the thalamus, and thalamic neurons project directly to the cerebrum. The thalamus does not just pass the information on, it also processes that information. For example, the portion of the thalamus that receives visual information will influence what visual stimuli are important, or what receives attention. The cerebrum also sends information down to the thalamus, which usually communicates motor commands.

Inferior and slightly anterior to the thalamus is the hypothalamus, the other major region of the diencephalon. The hypothalamus is a collection of nuclei that are largely involved in regulating homeostasis. The hypothalamus is the executive region in charge of the autonomic nervous system and the endocrine system through its regulation of the anterior pituitary gland. Other parts of the hypothalamus are involved in memory and emotion as part of the limbic system, and in the control of circadian (day/night) rhythms.

The Brain Stem. The brain stem includes three regions: the midbrain, the pons, and the medulla.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
The Brain Stem

The midbrain, and pons and the medulla oblongata of the hindbrain, are collectively referred to as the brain stem. The structure emerges from the ventral surface of the forebrain and connects the brain to the spinal cord. Attached to the brain stem, but considered a separate region of the adult brain, is the cerebellum.

Midbrain. Adapted from: Images are generated by Life Science Databases(LSDB), CC BY-SA 2.1 JP, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
The Midbrain

One of the original regions of the embryonic brain, the midbrain is a small region between the thalamus of the diencephalon and the pons. 

The midbrain includes four bumps known as the colliculi (singular = colliculus, which means “little hill” in Latin). The inferior colliculi are the inferior pair of these enlargements and are part of the auditory brain stem pathway. Neurons of the inferior colliculus project to the thalamus, which then sends auditory information to the cerebrum for the conscious perception of sound. The inferior colliculi also have a role in auditory reflexes, such as the startle response to loud sounds. 

The superior colliculi are the superior pair and combine sensory information about visual space, auditory space, and somatosensory space. Activity in the superior colliculi is related to orienting the eyes to a sound or touch stimulus. If you are walking along the sidewalk on campus and you hear chirping, the superior colliculi coordinates that information with your awareness of the visual location of the tree right above you. That is the correlation of auditory and visual maps.

slides.title: Part 3: The central nervous system
slides.body:
Part 3: The central nervous system

Dopaminergic system of the ventral tegmental area (VTA) and substantia nigra, pars compacta (SNc). Credit: Oscar Arias-Carrión, Xanic Caraza-Santiago, Sergio Salgado-Licona, Mohamed Salama, Sergio Machado, Antonio Egidio Nardi, Manuel Menéndez-González and Eric Murillo-Rodríguez., CC BY 4.0 <https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0>, via Wikimedia Commons

Midbrain

produces dopamine
axons travel out of midbrain and releases dopamine into basal nuclei of forebrain
Parkinson’s disease is due to loss of these neurons
ventral tegmental area (VTA)
involved in motivation & reward
releases dopamine into prefrontal cortex and nucleus accumbens
involved in drug addiction

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
The midbrain also contains arguably the most important sites of dopamine production in the brain, the ventral tegmental area and the substantia nigra. 

The substantia nigra, named because of black pigmentation within it, produces dopamine in neurons whose axons then extend out of the midbrain and travel to the basal nuclei of the forebrain, where the dopamine is released. Parkinson’s disease is caused by a loss of these neurons, and thus insufficient dopamine release within the basal nuclei, which we have already discussed as having a role in motor control of the body.

The ventral tegmental area produces dopamine, and its neurons travel out of the midbrain and target areas of the prefrontal cortex and a nucleus called the nucleus accumbens. The ventral tegmental area, and its dopamine, is heavily involved in our motivational and reward processes, which help drive us toward behaviors necessary for life (e.g., eating), and then provide a reward for doing so (e.g., pleasure associated with eating favored foods). Unfortunately, illegal drug use is problematic because many drugs classes target this pathway and enhance dopamine release within regions like the nucleus accumbens, or they cause dopamine to remain in those regions longer. Over time, the body downregulates receptors for dopamine in those regions to counter the overstimulation, and then higher doses of drugs are needed to achieve comparable rewarding effects. This spiral, and the addictiveness of these drugs, can have extremely serious consequences.

Ascending input from the periphery and spinal cord enters through the fibers of the inferior olive. Output goes to the midbrain, which sends a descending signal to the spinal cord.

Pons

The word pons comes from the Latin word for bridge. It is visible on the anterior surface of the brain stem as the thick bundle of white matter attached to the cerebellum. The pons is the main connection between the cerebellum and the brain stem.

Medulla oblongata. Adapted from: Images are generated by Life Science Databases(LSDB), CC BY-SA 2.1 JP, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Medulla

The medulla, also known as the medulla oblongata, contains autonomic nuclei with motor neurons that control the rate and force of heart contraction, the diameter of blood vessels and the rate and depth of breathing, among other essential physiological processes. The grey matter of the medulla also connects with the grey matter of the midbrain and pons to form the reticular formation, a system that regulates various bodily functions. Within the formation is the reticular activating system, whose functions include the control of sleep and wakefulness, general brain activity and attention.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
The Cerebellum

The cerebellum, as the name suggests, is the “little brain.” It is covered in gyri and sulci like the cerebrum, and looks like a miniature version of that part of the brain. The cerebellum integrates motor commands from the cerebral cortex with sensory feedback from the periphery, allowing for the coordination and precise execution of motor activities, such as walking, cycling, or playing a musical instrument.

The Spinal Cord

The length of the spinal cord is divided into regions that correspond to the regions of the vertebral column. Immediately adjacent to the brain stem is the cervical region, followed by the thoracic, then the lumbar, and finally the sacral and coccygeal regions.

Cross-section of Spinal Cord. The cross-section of a thoracic spinal cord segment shows the posterior, anterior, and lateral horns of grey matter, as well as the posterior, anterior, and lateral columns of white matter. LM × 40. (Micrograph provided by the Regents of University of Michigan Medical School © 2012)

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
In cross-section, the grey matter of the spinal cord has the appearance of an ink-blot test, with the spread of the grey matter on one side replicated on the other—a shape reminiscent of a bulbous capital “H.” As shown in the figure, the grey matter is subdivided into regions that are referred to as horns.

The dorsal (or posterior) horn is responsible for sensory processing. The ventral (or anterior) horn sends out motor signals to the skeletal muscles. The lateral horn, which is only found in the thoracic, upper lumbar, and sacral regions, is the central component of the sympathetic division of the autonomic nervous system.

Just as the grey matter is separated into horns, the white matter of the spinal cord is separated into columns. Ascending tracts of nervous system fibres in these columns carry sensory information up to the brain, whereas descending tracts carry efferent motor commands from the brain.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
The Meninges

The outer surface of the central nervous system is covered by a series of membranes composed of connective tissue called the meninges, which protect the brain. The dura mater is a thick fibrous layer and a strong protective sheath over the entire brain and spinal cord. It is anchored to the inner surface of the cranium and vertebral cavity. The arachnoid mater is a membrane of thin fibrous tissue that forms a loose sac around the central nervous system. Beneath the arachnoid is a thin, filamentous mesh called the arachnoid trabeculae, which looks like a spider web, giving this layer its name. Directly adjacent to the surface of the central nervous system is the pia mater, a thin fibrous membrane that follows the convolutions of gyri and sulci in the cerebral cortex and fits into other grooves and indentations.

slides.title: Part 3: The central nervous system
slides.body:

Ventricular system and cerebrospinal fluid circulation
cerebrospinal fluid (CSF)
produced by network of cells (ependymal glia) that filters blood, called choroid plexus
circulates throughout ventricles (open spaces) of CNS 
removes metabolic wastes from the interstitial fluids
then emerges into subarachnoid space and reabsorbed into blood

Cerebrospinal Fluid Circulation. The choroid plexus in the four ventricles produce CSF, which is circulated through the ventricular system and then enters the subarachnoid space through the median and lateral apertures. The CSF is then reabsorbed into the blood at the arachnoid granulations, where the arachnoid membrane emerges into the dural sinuses.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
The Ventricular System and Cerebrospinal Fluid Circulation

Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) circulates throughout and around the central nervous system. Specifically, cerebrospinal fluid circulates to remove metabolic wastes from the interstitial fluids of nervous tissues and return them to the blood stream. The ventricles are the open spaces within the brain where cerebrospinal fluid circulates. In some of these spaces, cerebrospinal fluid is produced by filtering of the blood that is performed by a specialized network of cells known as a choroid plexus. The cerebrospinal fluid circulates through all of the ventricles to eventually emerge into the subarachnoid space where it will be reabsorbed into the blood.

Human ventricular system. Adapted from: BodyParts3D[1] by DBCLS., CC BY-SA 2.1 JP, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes: There are four ventricles within the brain, all of which develop from the original hollow space within the neural tube, the central canal. The first two are named the lateral ventricles and are deep within the cerebrum. These ventricles are connected to the third ventricle by two openings called the interventricular foramina. The third ventricle is the space between the left and right sides of the diencephalon, which opens into the cerebral aqueduct that passes through the midbrain. The aqueduct opens into the fourth ventricle, which is the space between the cerebellum and the pons and upper medulla.

~500 ml made per day

Brain dissection showing choroid plexus in leteral ventricles. Credit: Anatomist90, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
As mentioned, cerebrospinal fluid is produced within the ventricles by a type of specialized membrane called a choroid plexus. Ependymal cells (a type of glial cell) surround blood capillaries and filter the blood to make cerebrospinal fluid. The fluid is a clear solution with a limited amount of the constituents of blood. It is essentially water, small molecules, and electrolytes. Oxygen and carbon dioxide are dissolved into the cerebrospinal fluid, as they are in blood, and can diffuse between the fluid and the nervous tissue.

The choroid plexuses are found in all four ventricles. Observed in dissection, they appear as soft, fuzzy structures that may still be pink, depending on how well the circulatory system is cleared in preparation of the tissue. The cerebrospinal fluid is produced from components extracted from the blood, so its flow out of the ventricles is tied to the pulse of cardiovascular circulation.

single median aperture and pair of lateral apertures

Cerebrospinal Fluid Circulation. The choroid plexus in the four ventricles produce CSF, which is circulated through the ventricular system and then enters the subarachnoid space through the median and lateral apertures. The CSF is then reabsorbed into the blood at the arachnoid granulations, where the arachnoid membrane emerges into the dural sinuses.

Human ventricular system. Adapted from: BodyParts3D[1] by DBCLS., CC BY-SA 2.1 JP, via Wikimedia Commons

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Cerebrospinal Fluid Circulation

From the lateral ventricles, the CSF flows into the third ventricle, where more CSF is produced, and then through the cerebral aqueduct into the fourth ventricle where even more CSF is produced. From the fourth ventricle, the cerebrospinal fluid can continue down the central canal of the spinal cord, but this is essentially a cul-de-sac, so more of the fluid leaves the ventricular system and moves into the subarachnoid space through the median and lateral apertures.

Cerebrospinal Fluid Circulation. The choroid plexus in the four ventricles produce CSF, which is circulated through the ventricular system and then enters the subarachnoid space through the median and lateral apertures. The CSF is then reabsorbed into the blood at the arachnoid granulations, where the arachnoid membrane emerges into the dural sinuses.

THOMPSON RIVERS UNIVERSITY | 2024
slides.notes:
Within the subarachnoid space, the cerebrospinal fluid flows around all of the central nervous system, providing two important functions. As with elsewhere in its circulation, the cerebrospinal fluid picks up metabolic wastes from the nervous tissue and moves it out of the central nervous system. It also acts as a liquid cushion for the brain and spinal cord. By surrounding the entire system in the subarachnoid space, it provides a thin buffer around the organs within the strong, protective dura mater. 

The arachnoid granulations are outpocketings of the arachnoid membrane into the dural sinuses so that cerebrospinal fluid can be reabsorbed into the blood, along with the metabolic wastes. From the dural sinuses, blood drains out of the head and neck through the jugular veins, along with the rest of the circulation, for blood to be re-oxygenated by the lungs and wastes to be filtered out by the kidneys.
